learn.hook: A small village pond has fish, frogs, water lilies, dragonflies, sunlight, mud and water, all working together like one big team!
points: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with the non-living things around them.
Living (biotic) parts include plants, animals and microorganisms. Non-living (abiotic) parts include sunlight, air, water, soil, minerals and temperature.
Ecosystems can be large or small: a forest, a grassland, a desert, a pond, a sea, or even a rotting log.
India has many ecosystems: the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, the rainforests of the Western Ghats, the Thar Desert and Chilika Lake in Odisha.
The living things in an ecosystem are suited (adapted) to its non-living conditions, like camels to the hot, dry desert.

example.q: Think it through: In a school garden there are neem trees, earthworms, sparrows, soil, sunlight and rainwater. Sort them into living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
steps: Living things grow, need food and reproduce: neem trees, earthworms and sparrows.
Non-living parts do not do these things: soil, sunlight and rainwater.
Together, and interacting, they form the garden ecosystem.
example.answer: Living: neem trees, earthworms, sparrows. Non-living: soil, sunlight, rainwater.

learn.reallife: Mangrove forests in the Sundarbans protect the coast from storms and are home to the Royal Bengal tiger, crabs, fish and many birds.

quiz.q: What is an ecosystem?
options: Living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings
Only the animals of a forest
Only the soil and rocks of a place
quiz.explain: An ecosystem includes both living and non-living parts and how they interact.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an ecosystem has only living things

quiz.q: Which is an abiotic (non-living) part of a pond ecosystem?
quiz.explain: Water is non-living; fish, algae and ducks are living.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up biotic and abiotic parts

quiz.q: Which of these is a biotic (living) part of a forest?
quiz.explain: Fungi are living decomposers. Sunlight, air and rocks are non-living.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that fungi and microbes are living parts of an ecosystem

quiz.q: The Sundarbans is famous for which type of ecosystem?
quiz.explain: The Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta has the largest mangrove forest in the world.
quiz.mistake: Does not know India's major ecosystems

quiz.q: Can a single rotting log be called an ecosystem?
options: Yes, it has living things like fungi and insects interacting with moisture, air and wood
No, ecosystems must be very big
Only if a tiger lives there
quiz.explain: Ecosystems can be small. A log has its own community of organisms and non-living conditions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only large areas are ecosystems

quiz.q: Why can a camel survive well in the Thar Desert?
options: It is adapted to hot, dry conditions
Camels do not need water ever
quiz.explain: Camels can go long periods without drinking and have features suited to heat and sand.
quiz.mistake: Thinks camels never need water

quiz.q: Which is NOT an ecosystem?
options: A plastic bottle kept empty on a shelf
quiz.explain: An empty bottle has no community of living things interacting, so it is not an ecosystem.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any place or object is an ecosystem

quiz.q: Which pair shows a living thing and a non-living factor that it needs?
quiz.explain: A plant (living) needs sunlight (non-living) to make food. The other pairs are both non-living.
quiz.mistake: Does not separate living and non-living parts correctly

teach.ask: Gappu looks at a pond: My teacher says this pond is an ecosystem. But it is just water! What is an ecosystem?
teach.praise: An ecosystem is living things like fish and plants interacting with non-living things like water and sunlight. My pond is a whole world!
teach.nudge: Is the pond only water? What living and non-living things are there, and what do they do together?

learn.hook: The energy in the muscles of a tiger chasing a deer in Kanha started out as sunlight falling on a blade of grass!
points: Green plants are producers: they make their own food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide (photosynthesis).
Consumers eat other living things. Herbivores eat plants (deer), carnivores eat animals (tiger), and omnivores eat both (bear, crow, humans).
A food chain shows who eats whom, with arrows pointing towards the eater: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.
Energy passes along the chain, but much of it is used for living and lost as heat at each step. Only a small part (about 10%) passes to the next level, so food chains are usually short.
In nature, food chains link together to form a food web. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead remains at every level and return nutrients to the soil.

example.q: Think it through: In the chain grass → deer → tiger, which is the producer, which is the herbivore and which is the carnivore? Where does the energy begin?
steps: Grass makes its own food using sunlight: producer.
The deer eats grass: herbivore (primary consumer).
The tiger eats deer: carnivore (secondary consumer).
The energy begins with sunlight captured by the grass.
example.answer: Grass is the producer, deer the herbivore and tiger the carnivore; the energy comes from the Sun.

learn.reallife: A garden with many kinds of plants supports more insects, birds and lizards, because many food chains link into a strong food web.

games.title: Build the food chain
games.prompt: Put the food chain in order, from producer to top consumer

quiz.q: In a food chain, the producer is usually a:
quiz.explain: Green plants make their own food from sunlight, so they start food chains.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any living thing can be a producer

quiz.q: In the chain grass → rabbit → fox, the rabbit is a:
quiz.explain: The rabbit eats plants (grass), so it is a herbivore, or primary consumer.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the levels of a food chain

quiz.q: In a food chain, the arrow points from:
options: The decomposer to the producer only
quiz.explain: Arrows show the direction in which food and energy move: towards the eater.
quiz.mistake: Draws arrows from predator to prey

quiz.q: What is the original source of energy for almost all food chains?
quiz.explain: Plants capture sunlight in photosynthesis; this energy then passes along the chain.
quiz.mistake: Thinks plants get their energy from soil

quiz.q: Which of these is an omnivore?
quiz.explain: A bear eats both plants (fruits, honey) and animals (insects, fish).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up herbivores, carnivores and omnivores

quiz.q: What do decomposers like bacteria and fungi do?
options: Break down dead remains and return nutrients to the soil
quiz.explain: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead plants and animals so producers can use them again.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand the role of decomposers

quiz.q: A field's grass holds 10,000 units of energy. Roughly how many units reach the grasshoppers that eat it (about 10%)?
steps: About 10% passes to the next level
quiz.explain: Most energy is used or lost as heat at each level, so only about a tenth moves up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all the energy passes to the next level

quiz.q: Many food chains linked together in an ecosystem make a:
quiz.explain: Animals usually eat more than one kind of food, so food chains join up into a web.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term food web

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: I eat worms, and the cat wants to eat me! How does energy travel from the Sun to the cat?
teach.praise: Plants capture the Sun's energy, then it passes to consumers who eat them, step by step along the food chain. Please, cat, look the other way!
teach.nudge: Who catches the Sun's energy first? And how does it move from one living thing to the next?

learn.hook: No bees, no mangoes? It is true! Many fruit trees need bees and other insects to carry pollen from flower to flower.
points: Living things depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal. This is called interdependence.
Plants give oxygen and food; animals breathe out carbon dioxide that plants use. Bees and butterflies pollinate flowers, and birds and animals spread seeds.
Decomposers break down dead matter, recycling nutrients so new plants can grow.
If one population changes, others are affected. If frogs disappear from a field, insects may increase while snakes that eat frogs may decrease.
A balanced ecosystem has many kinds of living things. Human activities like cutting forests, pollution and overfishing can upset this balance.

example.q: Think it through: Farmers in a village kill most of the snakes in their fields. What might happen to the rats, and to the crops?
steps: With fewer snakes, fewer rats are eaten, so the rat population grows.
More rats eat more grain, so crop damage increases.
example.answer: Rats would increase and damage more crops, showing how removing one species upsets the balance.

learn.reallife: When vulture numbers fell sharply in India, dead animals were left lying for longer. Vultures are nature's clean-up crew, so their loss affected the whole ecosystem.

games.title: Who helps whom?
pairs: Bird eating fruit and dropping seeds

games.title: Balance check
items: Removing one species from an ecosystem can affect many others.
Living things are linked through food chains and other relationships.
Plants depend on animals for pollination and seed dispersal.
Many plants rely on insects, birds and animals for these.
Decomposers are not needed in an ecosystem.
Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would not be recycled.
An ecosystem with many kinds of living things is usually more stable.
If one food source fails, animals can switch to others.
Animals depend on plants, but plants never depend on animals.
Plants depend on animals for pollination, seed dispersal and the carbon dioxide they breathe out.

quiz.q: What is interdependence in an ecosystem?
options: Living things depending on each other
quiz.explain: Organisms rely on each other for food, shelter, pollination and more.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand the term interdependence

quiz.q: How do bees help plants?
quiz.explain: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, helping plants form fruits and seeds.
quiz.mistake: Does not know about pollination

quiz.q: If all frogs vanished from a paddy field, what is most likely to happen?
quiz.explain: Frogs eat insects, so without frogs, insect numbers would rise.
quiz.mistake: Does not trace effects through a food chain

quiz.q: In the same field, what would likely happen to the snakes that eat frogs?
quiz.explain: With less food available, the snake population would likely fall.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that predators depend on their prey

quiz.q: Which shows plants and animals depending on each other for gases?
options: Plants release oxygen; animals breathe out carbon dioxide
Plants breathe out carbon dioxide for animals to make food
quiz.explain: Animals use oxygen from plants; plants use carbon dioxide in photosynthesis.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the exchange of gases

quiz.q: A bird eats a jamun and drops the seed far away, where a new tree grows. This is:
quiz.explain: Animals spreading seeds to new places is seed dispersal.
quiz.mistake: Confuses seed dispersal with pollination

quiz.q: Which human activity most upsets the balance of a forest ecosystem?
options: Cutting down large areas of trees
quiz.explain: Deforestation destroys homes and food of many organisms at once.
quiz.mistake: Does not identify harmful human activities

quiz.q: Why are vultures important in an ecosystem?
quiz.explain: Vultures feed on carcasses, cleaning up the environment and helping prevent the spread of disease.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the role of scavengers

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: Why should I care about bees and frogs? I am a bird! Do living things really need each other?
teach.praise: Living things depend on each other for food, pollination and more, so if one disappears, the balance is upset. I will protect my bee friends!
teach.nudge: Do bees, plants and frogs need each other? What happens to others if one of them disappears?
